Performance Monitoring

1. Performance Monitoring

“The server is slow” is an observation to refine, not a diagnosis. HarborStatus can miss a response target because of CPU contention, memory pressure, storage latency, network loss, or an upstream dependency. Useful performance work connects a user-visible symptom to measurements collected over the same interval.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — Chapter 22 — Performance Monitoring

2. Measure demand against service outcomes

Measure representative intervals and correlate resource observations with service outcomes. One counter is not a root cause. A single high load average is treated as proof of CPU saturation.

SOURCE: Measure demand against service outcomes

3. Chapter 22 — Performance Monitoring

“The server is slow” is an observation to refine, not a diagnosis. HarborStatus can miss a response target because of CPU contention, memory pressure, storage latency, network loss, or an upstream dependency. Useful performance work connects a user-visible symptom to measurements collected over the same interval.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — Chapter 22 — Performance Monitoring

4. 22.1 Establishing a Baseline

A baseline describes a known workload and the system’s behavior under it. Record request rate, response-time distribution, errors, CPU use, memory availability, storage latency, network traffic, and configuration. A quiet midnight sample is not a valid baseline for a busy morning simply because it is older.

Capture units and sampling intervals. A value without a timestamp, host, workload, and measurement definition is difficult to compare. Keep ordinary and peak periods, deployment markers, and relevant growth trends. For teaching, five minutes of a controlled workload can be useful; production baselines must represent the service’s actual operating cycle.

Change one variable at a time when conducting an experiment. Otherwise an improvement cannot be attributed confidently to a specific change. Preserve the original state and test that any performance gain does not come from dropping work or returning incorrect answers.

Linux example — 22.1

Collect a dated baseline with bounded samples.

What to check: Record workload conditions so a later comparison is meaningful.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — 22.1 Establishing a Baseline

6. 22.2 CPU Performance

CPU utilization describes time spent executing particular classes of work. It does not directly describe useful application throughput. A tight retry loop can consume a core while completing nothing. A mostly idle machine can still have one saturated thread that limits the application.

Inspect per-core as well as aggregate use. Correlate user time, system time, runnable tasks, and application latency. In a VM, steal time can indicate that the guest wanted CPU time the host was serving elsewhere; its interpretation depends on the platform and counters available.

Do not equate a load average of four with 400 percent CPU use. Load and utilization measure different things. Determine whether tasks are runnable or waiting in relevant uninterruptible states, then examine the resource actually delaying completion.

Linux example — 22.2

Sample CPU use when sysstat is installed.

What to check: Per-CPU imbalance can disappear in a host-wide average; use -P ALL when needed.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — 22.2 CPU Performance

8. 22.3 Memory Performance

Linux uses otherwise idle memory for cache, so low “free” memory does not alone indicate an emergency. Inspect available memory, reclaim, swap activity, process growth, and pressure over time. A large cache may be helping the workload.

Resident memory describes pages currently resident for a process, but summing every process’s resident set can double-count shared pages. A virtual size can include reserved address space that is not physically occupied. Choose the measure that answers the question instead of ranking processes by whichever column looks largest.

A cgroup-limited service can hit its limit while the host still has abundant memory. Inspect the service’s effective controls and memory events alongside host totals. The correct response might be fixing a leak, reducing concurrency, or revising a tested limit—not adding swap by reflex. (R16)

Linux example — 22.3

Compare available memory and paging activity.

What to check: Interpret later interval samples for swap-in/out rather than treating low free memory alone as exhaustion.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — 22.3 Memory Performance

10. 22.4 Disk Performance

Storage performance includes throughput, operations per second, latency, and queueing. A sequential archive transfer and a database performing small synchronous writes stress storage differently. The device, filesystem, controller, virtualization layer, and remote backend can each impose constraints.

A high queue and rising latency during stable demand suggest contention, but no universal numeric threshold proves the cause. Modern devices can perform several requests in parallel. In particular, a utilization percentage near 100 is not a complete saturation verdict for every NVMe device or RAID array.

Separate capacity from performance. A filesystem can have free space and still be slow; a full filesystem can fail writes even when latency looked normal moments earlier. Also inspect error messages because retries on failing hardware can resemble ordinary load.

Linux example — 22.4

Sample disk latency and activity.

What to check: The first report is cumulative since boot; later samples reflect the interval.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — 22.4 Disk Performance

12. 22.5 Network Performance

Measure application transfer rate together with errors, drops, retransmissions, connection behavior, and end-to-end latency. Link speed is a nominal capability, not a guarantee of throughput between two applications. Routing, congestion, encryption, receiver speed, and storage may be the actual constraints.

Compare counter changes over a measured interval rather than treating lifetime totals as current rates. A nonzero error counter dating from installation may be unrelated to the incident. Packet captures can provide stronger evidence but require authorization, bounded scope, and protection against exposing credentials or payloads.

A successful ping is a useful narrow result, not a test of every transport port or application exchange. It can succeed while HTTPS fails, or be blocked while the application works.

Linux example — 22.5

Read interface counters.

What to check: Drops and errors need rate and baseline comparisons; cumulative totals are not a current throughput measurement.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — 22.5 Network Performance

15. 22.6 free

free -h presents a human-readable summary of memory and swap. For a repeatable parser, use a defined unit and a stable locale or a structured source rather than parsing values that switch between MiB and GiB.

The second invocation samples repeatedly on implementations supporting those options. Look for trends and correlate with workload. “Available” is an estimate of memory usable for new applications without swapping, not a promise that every future allocation will succeed under all policies.

Do not clear caches as a routine way to make the output look cleaner. That changes the workload’s environment and can worsen performance while hiding the reason the cache was useful.

Linux example — 22.6

Read human-readable memory accounting.

What to check: Available memory estimates what can be used without swapping; cache has a separate role.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — 22.6 free

18. 22.7 vmstat

vmstat combines observations about runnable and blocked tasks, memory, swap, I/O, interrupts, and CPU. A short interval series is often more useful than a single display:

For common procps implementations, the first report includes averages since boot for rate-based fields; later reports describe intervals. Read the header and installed manual. Sustained swap-in and swap-out together with latency can support a memory-pressure hypothesis, but distinguish historical swap occupancy from current paging activity. (R15)

Use vmstat to decide which layer deserves closer inspection, not to assign a cause from one column. A high runnable count with low application progress is a different investigation from blocked tasks alongside storage errors.

Linux example — 22.7

Sample scheduler, memory, and I/O state.

What to check: Compare runnable and blocked tasks with CPU and I/O fields.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — 22.7 vmstat

21. 22.8 iostat

The sysstat iostat tool reports CPU and block-device statistics. An extended interval view is a useful starting point:

The installed version determines column names. Common fields include request rates, throughput, average completion time, queue measures, and utilization. -z suppresses inactive devices in supported versions; it should not hide a device you intended to observe without checking why it is absent.

Map the application’s filesystem through its logical volumes and devices. A statistic for a physical device can aggregate several unrelated workloads. Observe both the logical path and underlying devices when the mapping is important. Avoid double-counting the same I/O across stacked layers. (R52)

Linux example — 22.8

Observe extended block-device statistics.

What to check: High utilization on modern storage is not alone proof of saturation; inspect latency and workload limits.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — 22.8 iostat

24. 22.9 sar

sar reads current or retained system-activity measurements collected by sysstat. Historical data is valuable when the incident ended before an administrator connected, but only if collection was enabled and retained at a useful interval.

A command such as sar -u 1 5 samples CPU activity; retained-file queries depend on the package’s collection paths and schedule. Confirm the host, date, time zone, and sampling coverage before comparing events. A file named for a day number can be misunderstood after rotation.

A historical gap is missing evidence, not a period of zero load. Configure retention and collection overhead deliberately, then test retrieval during a drill rather than discovering during an incident that no history exists. (R52)

Linux example — 22.9

Take live CPU samples using sar.

What to check: Historical sar files require an enabled collection service; live sampling does not create a full historical baseline.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — 22.9 sar

26. 22.10 pidstat

pidstat attributes selected resource use to processes and, with appropriate options, threads. It helps connect a host-level symptom to an application rather than blaming the largest familiar process.

Use a specific PID where practical to reduce volume. A short-lived process may disappear between samples, and process IDs can be reused. Record the executable, start context, and service association alongside the PID. Compare the same interval as your system and application metrics. (R52)

Process-attributed disk activity and device-level completed I/O need not match exactly because caching and writeback affect attribution and timing. Treat differences as an observation to explain, not automatically as a broken tool.

Linux example — 22.10

Sample per-process resource use.

What to check: Requires sysstat; correlate high usage with the process's actual work.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — 22.10 pidstat

29. 22.11 iotop

iotop can show task-oriented I/O observations where the kernel and installed implementation provide the required accounting. Privileges or kernel settings can limit available detail. Read its warnings rather than assuming a blank display proves no I/O.

Observe for a bounded interval on the affected host. Buffered writes may be completed later by kernel writeback, so the application visible in a process display may not be the process currently issuing all physical requests. Combine task observations with device statistics and the application’s own workload.

Do not enable expensive accounting globally during an incident without understanding the effect. Start with existing counters and escalate measurement deliberately.

Linux example — 22.11

Observe process I/O if iotop is available.

What to check: Kernel support and privilege requirements vary; three reports keep the observation bounded.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — 22.11 iotop

31. 22.12 lsof

lsof relates processes to open files and sockets. This is valuable for identifying who keeps a filesystem busy, which process owns a listener, or which unlinked file still consumes space.

This lists open files with a link count below one on common Linux implementations. Scope investigation to the affected process or mount when the host is large. The command can be expensive or encounter inaccessible resources; review errors and avoid assuming an incomplete listing is exhaustive.

Closing the relevant descriptor releases a deleted file’s storage when no other references retain it. That may require a supported log-reopen signal or controlled restart. Deleting the name again cannot close a descriptor a process already owns.

Linux example — 22.12

Find open references to deleted files.

What to check: A deleted file can still consume blocks while a process holds it open; restarting requires a service-specific plan.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — 22.12 lsof

34. 22.13 /proc

/proc exposes live process and kernel information. Files such as /proc/meminfo, /proc/loadavg, and per-process status records support many higher-level tools. They are interfaces, not ordinary persistent files to copy back during recovery.

Pressure Stall Information, when available, measures time tasks are stalled on a resource. It can help explain why an application is slow even when a coarse utilization measure looks unremarkable. Availability and cgroup scope depend on kernel configuration and permissions. (R53)

An individual read is a snapshot in a changing system. Values from separate reads need not represent exactly the same instant. Collect a time series rather than building a causal story from inconsistent one-off samples.

Linux example — 22.13

Read kernel counters directly.

What to check: These values are counters or instantaneous state; rates require time-separated samples.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — 22.13 /proc

37. 22.14 Identifying Bottlenecks

A bottleneck is the constraint limiting useful progress for a particular workload. It is not necessarily the resource with the largest utilization percentage. Reducing one bottleneck can expose another, and a dependency outside the host can dominate the result.

Form a hypothesis with a predicted observation. “Storage is delaying requests” predicts aligned storage latency, waiting tasks, and application delay under the relevant workload. “The application serializes work” predicts a hot thread or lock behavior despite available host capacity.

Test the smallest reversible change that discriminates among explanations. Preserve correctness checks. Doubling throughput by skipping validation or returning cached stale answers is not an improvement unless the service contract permits it.

Linux example — 22.14

Compare CPU, memory, and disk observations.

What to check: Correlate timestamps and application latency; one busy resource may be a symptom of another constraint.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — 22.14 Identifying Bottlenecks

39. 22.15 Capacity Planning

Capacity planning connects expected demand, measured resource use, growth, and failure reserves. Include peak demand and the capacity remaining when a node or zone is unavailable. Average utilization alone can conceal burst-driven failures.

For a simple teaching estimate, a storage tree growing 2 GiB per day with 40 GiB usable headroom has about twenty days before reaching that limit under constant growth. Real growth may not be linear, and operational reserve must be deducted. The calculation is a prompt for action, not a guarantee of the exact exhaustion date.

Document assumptions and revisit them after releases or traffic changes. Scaling also changes licensing, cost, coordination, recovery, and operating complexity. Prefer evidence-based forecasts with ranges over a single precise-looking date unsupported by the data.

Linux example — 22.15

Record capacity and CPU count.

What to check: Trend workload growth and headroom over time rather than extrapolating from one idle snapshot.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — 22.15 Capacity Planning

41. Requirement

Distinguish a CPU-bound explanation from an I/O-bound explanation using a short, aligned observation window. Do not generate stress on production. The following values are invented teaching observations, not measured results from this book’s preparation.

During the same sixty-second incident window, suppose HarborStatus’s 95th-percentile response time rises from 120 ms to 1,800 ms. CPU remains mostly idle, device completion latency rises sharply, vmstat shows blocked tasks, and a backup transfer starts at the same time.

The simplest reaction is to add CPU because the website is slow. Its limitation is that it does not address the observed waiting path. The evidence supports investigating storage contention, but temporal correlation alone does not prove the backup is the cause.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — Requirement

42. Observation sequence

These sequential commands do not create perfectly simultaneous samples. For a strict comparison, use existing timestamped monitoring or start bounded collectors in a coordinated window. Note this limitation in the report rather than claiming more synchronization than the commands provide.

Inspect the backup schedule, target device mapping, storage errors, and request-time records. In a representative lab or approved window, compare normal workload with and without the competing transfer. Rate limiting or rescheduling might help, but test the backup’s RPO and completion time after the change.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — Observation sequence

43. Observation sequence · example 1

44. Verification

The expected result is improved client latency without lost requests, corrupted output, or a missed backup requirement. Preserve before-and-after measurements and the rollback. A CPU chart that looks calmer is not the acceptance criterion; the service contract is.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — Verification

45. Practice and implementation lab

Collect a five-minute baseline from an idle lab VM and from a harmless known workload. Explain which values are instantaneous, interval-based, cumulative, or estimates. Do not invent missing metrics when a utility is unavailable; record the coverage gap.

Check your understanding. Does low free memory prove a leak? No. Does one saturated core disappear in a many-core average? It can. Is the busiest-looking resource necessarily the bottleneck? No.

Chapter takeaway. Diagnose performance with aligned workload evidence, then judge changes by useful, correct service outcomes.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch024.xhtml — Practice and implementation lab

46. Correlate resource pressure with service latency

Correlation in invented samples narrows an investigation; it does not prove causation. The solution checks the stated outcome explicitly. These fixture results do not establish that a real privileged service is configured correctly.

SOURCE: Correlate resource pressure with service latency
